passages.text: The Influence of Social Support, Social Affiliation, and Intrinsic Motivation for Increasing Underserved Youth's Physical Activity: A Social Climate-Based Intervention Study

The purpose of this study was to investigate the influences of intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and reciprocal social support for physical activity (PA) on underserved youths' afterschool period moderate-to-vigorous (MVPA) changing trajectories across the 16-week Connect through PLAY intervention, a social-motivational climate intervention. A total of 113 youth (61.06% African American, 56.64% girls) provided full data. Youths' intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations and social support were measured by youth responses to a set of surveys at baseline and post-intervention. Youths' afterschool period MVPA was measured using data from 7-day ActiGraph accelerometer wear at baseline, midpoint, and post-intervention. Hierarchical linear modeling analysis found that youth daily afterschool period (3pm-6pm) MVPA increased, on average, 37.94 minutes across the 16-week intervention. Increases in intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations and social support were positive predictors of youth afterschool MVPA changing trajectory. The findings clarify the contributions that a social-motivational climate intervention can have on youth afterschool period MVPA through increasing youth intrinsic motivation, social affiliation, and reciprocal social support.
Introduction

Although schools are charged with providing opportunities for daily physical activity (PA) accrual throughout the day to promote health and wellbeing, the demands of basic classroom instruction, testing, and administration, impede the ability of schools to provide PA opportunities and thus, leave the majority of youth (between the ages of 9 to 15 years old) falling short of the recommended 60 minutes of daily moderate to vigorous (MV)PA. Consequently, the hours that immediately follow the school day, often referred to as the "after school hours" (i.e., 3 to 6pm) have been identified as a critical time to support youth PA. Youth within underserved communities face numerous contextual, familial, and personal barriers that impede daily MVPA accrual including lack of access to PA supportive practices, facility and equipment shortages, high afterschool program staff burn out rate, and expensive "pay-to-play" recreational activity models. These challenges are reflected in alarmingly low rates of MVPA among youth, with minoritized youth within underserved communities having the lowest levels of PA and the greatest declines in PA across these developmental years.

To address the paucity of PA time in schools, afterschool programs (ASPs) are targeted as important sites that focus on expanding PA throughout the school day. According to the recent American After 3PM report, over 7.8 million youth enroll in ASPs yearly, and these programs have a broad reach to under-resourced high-risk communities (low-socioeconomic conditions, minoritized). Typically, ASPs operate for approximately three hours following the end of a regular school day (most often from 3-6pm) and provide youth opportunities for PA as one component of a multi-activity daily curriculum. The national, state, and local PA standards and benchmarks recommend that youth need at least 30 minutes of afterschool program time dedicated to physical activity. However, a recent meta-analysis study revealed that ASPs are not meeting the minimal benchmarks identified in policy guidelines, with youth, on average, spending only 23.5min (and an average 11.7 min/hour) in MVPA during their ASP attendance.

Staff, peer, and activity-based factors influencing the PA social motivational climate have been proposed as critical determinants of youth MVPA accrual in ASPs. This includes the facilitation of positive staff-youth connections where program staff support, encourage, and engage with youth in MVPA, facilitate positive peer experiences, and a supportive social-motivational PA climate. Prior research has shown that a greater number of youth engage in MVPA when ASP staff encourage youth to be physically active and engage in physical activities with youth. Likewise, preliminary evidence from a social climate intervention indicates that focusing on improving the social experiences of PA opportunities within ASPs, including fostering inclusion, teamwork, youth sense of belonging and connection to peers and staff, is effective for improving youth MVPA accrual within ASPs. However, little-to-no research has examined the intrapersonal social-motivational mechanisms by which a social climate-based intervention impacts PA behavior. Understanding social motivational changes that account for behavior change are key for developing PA programming that supports sustained improvements in MVPA among youth.
Social-Motivational Climate Approach for Promoting Youth PA

The social-motivational climate approach for this study is based on a novel theoretical framework that expands on the social motivational constructs highlighted by Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Achievement Goal Theory (AGT). Guided by SDT, goal-directed behaviors should be stimulated in order to satisfy the basic human need for social connection and meaningful interpersonal relationships. AGT asserts that individuals want to and will strive to display competence in the way they define it and that youth commonly define PA competence as externally referenced and positive social connections as a primary motivator (and purpose) for initial and sustained PA behaviors and engagement (e.g., peer acceptance, close friendship, being part of a team, positive relationships with teachers, program staff and coaches). Therefore, facilitating and supporting social affiliation-based PA orientations that conceptualize PA competence in terms of developing positive relationships with others is perceived as a key motivational approach for promoting intrinsic motivation and sustained PA.

A social affiliation orientation toward PA is considered to be intrinsic and adaptive in nature because the social climate of PA can provide an individual with internally pleasing social experiences. In turn, these positive social experiences within youth settings further bolster social affiliation orientations towards PA. Previous research has demonstrated three specific components of a social affiliation orientation that are particularly representative of the types of social relationships important to youth within physical domains and can be nurtured by a positive PA setting: (1) Friendships and development of PA-based social skills; (2) Group Belonging and peer connection; and (3) Connection to positive and supportive adults through PA.

Provision of a positive PA social-climate that fosters friendship and connection also provides opportunities for youth to both give and receive social support for PA from others. The development of new social networks and reciprocal social support has been proposed by theory and previous empirical research as another effective intervention mechanism within social-climate interventions with social support from peers and teachers consistently shown to both facilitate and maintain youth PA. Although substantial research evidence indicates that social support and social motivations for PA can be effective mechanisms to target and facilitate within PA interventions for youth, there have been only a few youth-based PA interventions that have focused specifically on social climate elements (e.g.,) and no studies to our knowledge that have targeted social affiliation motivations for PA. Lack of attention towards social experiences and social motivations may be one reason why youth intervention approaches have had little impact on sustaining desired psychological, behavioral, and anthropometric (e.g., BMI) and physiological health outcomes. In fact, a number of qualitative studies have identified the presence of several interpersonal barriers (e.g., peer cliques, teasing) within youth interventions that impact ASP PA program effectiveness and the acceptability and sustainability of PA interventions. The limited empirical research on how to facilitate social goal orientations, reciprocal social support, and intrinsic motivation as key mechanisms to promote sustained PA in under-resourced ASPs call for more studies to examine the changing PA trajectory of at-risk youth who are enrolled in positive PA social climate-based ASP settings and to determine whether improvements in intrinsic and affiliation motivations, along with perceived social support resulting from a social-climate based intervention account for increases in underserved youth MVPA.
The Current Study

The current study set out to address these critical gaps in youth health promotion research by examining the impact of changes in social affiliation goals, intrinsic motivation, and social support on the MVPA trajectories of underserved youth who participated in a larger social climate-based intervention "Connect through Positive Leisure Activities for Youth (PLAY)". Guided by SDT and AGT, the purpose of this study was to fill the knowledge gap by investigating the influences of intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and perceived social support on underserved youths' afterschool period MVPA changing trajectories across a 16-week Connect through PLAY intervention. The two research questions that guided the present study are: (1) to what extent does youths' afterschool period MVPA change from baseline to endpoint during a 16-week social climate-based PA intervention within ASPs; (2) Does improvements in youth's intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations and social support across the 16-week intervention positively influence the 16-week trajectory of their afterschool period MVPA? It was hypothesized that participation in the Connect through PLAY intervention would result in significant increases in youth daily afterschool MVPA time from baseline to endpoint across the 16-week intervention. Observed improvements in youth's intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientation, and social support across the 16-week intervention were hypothesized to positively contribute to their afterschool hours MVPA.
Methods

The current study includes completed data collected from all intervention sites of the first and second year of an ongoing 5-year randomized controlled trial PA intervention research implemented within pre-existing afterschool programs (ASPs) from the Southeastern United States (South Carolina; 2018-2025; extension needed due to COVID-19). The intervention aims to improve staff capacity for implementing effective PA programming within ASPs serving underserved youth through addressing the social and motivational developmental needs of youth. During Y1 and Y2 (August 2018-March 2020) a total of 10 ASPs were randomly sampled with stratification criteria at site level. Inclusion criteria specified that sites had to be mid-sized ASPs (enrollment between 30-60 youth) with minimal enrollment fees ($0 - $50) and student enrollments of at least 50% of youth from underserved communities (defined by free/reduced lunch and minority status). The selected ASPs were randomly assigned to either the social development PA program intervention or active health curriculum control. Given the purpose of the current study, only data from the experimental condition were used because the social-motivational climate approach was not structured in the comparison condition. A repeated-measures design was used in this study.
The Intervention Curriculum

Connect through PLAY is a 16-week randomized controlled trial intervention study that focuses on facilitating three key social mechanisms for promoting youth PA within pre-existing ASPs that serve under-resourced communities: (a) Developing shared PA goals that are centered on developing close connections and friendships with others; (b) Establishing positive peer PA norms, that foster inclusiveness, and tangible social support within the PA context to promote group belonging; and (c) Enhancing ASP staff efficacy, activity involvement, and engagement to facilitate supportive staff-youth connections (Authors, 2021).

The three primary intervention components of Connect through PLAY are centered on facilitating these social mechanisms of the intervention. First, the Connect social motivational PA curriculum, which consists of "Connect the Dots" small group sessions (30 minutes per week) and a comprehensive set of novel "Connect PA" opportunities (never previously played by youth; 60 minutes/3 times per week), focuses on providing guided social opportunities, ensuring collaborative, inclusive play concentrated on fun and social goals, and producing positive social-emotional outcomes that staff could implement within ASPs. The second component, Staff Comprehensive Training, consists of four 2-hour training sessions that aim to build both strategies for developing positive connections and group belonging within ASPs as well as deliver detailed instructions for implementing the Connect PA curriculum materials. The third component, the Connect Staff Health Initiative, aims to empower staff to be positive PA role models and social supports for youth through theoretical and evidence-based strategies, that promote staff's own motivation, self-efficacy, and PA engagement by emphasizing autonomy support, relatedness support and behavioral skills such as self-monitoring, goal setting, skill-building, social support, and performance feedback. See for full details of the Connect intervention.
Participants

Data was collected from participants enrolled in 5 ASPs serving underserved youth. Prior to data collection, the Connect intervention team met with primary caregivers of all enrolled youth between the ages 9 through 16 through "Parent Night" events and one-on-one meetings at the ASP student sign-out table to describe the details of the study, provide caregivers the opportunity to ask any questions, and invite them to consent to have their child participate in the study measurements. All youth whose parents provided written informed consent were then asked if they would like to provide written assent to participate in the study. To be included in the study youth had to be currently enrolled in the ASP, have parental consent to participate, have agreed to study participation (assent), and be available for baseline and post-intervention measurement. Youth were excluded from participation only if they 1) had a medical condition that would interfere with the prescribed PA curriculum, 2) do not consistently attend the ASP (less than three days/wk), or 3) were in treatment for a psychiatric disorder or developmentally delayed such that the intervention/measurement materials would not be appropriate. In the current study, all youth in the sample received parent consent and provided their own assent to participate in the study. All procedures performed in this study were performed in accordance with the ethical standards of the American Psychological Association and were approved by the University of South Carolina institutional ethics committee (Pro00037559). The study participants were drawn from a group of 193 youth who had participated in the PA intervention condition between 2018 to 2020 of the 5-year trial from 5 APSs. Only the subsample of participants with completed data at baseline, midpoint, and endpoint were included in the analyses (N = 113). The final sample consisted of 43.36% boys (N = 49) and 56.64% girls (N = 64) from Grades 4 through 8 who were between the ages of 9 to 15 years old; average age was 11.29 (Standard Deviation = 1.06). The ethnicity composition of this sample was as follows: 61.06% (N = 69) identified as African American, 25.66% (N = 29) identified as European America, and 13.28% (N = 15) identified as multiracial, Asian, Pacific Islander or other. Chi-Square tests indicated that there were no differences by gender [chi2 (2, 193) = 5.52, p = .063], race [chi2 (3, 193) = 5.96, p = .11], or age [chi2 (6, 193) = 9.87, p = .13] between youth who were included in the data analysis and those who were excluded because they did not have complete data. Results also showed that there were no differences between those who had complete data and those who did not have complete data on baseline intrinsic motivation [chi2 (14, 193) = 25.14, p = .33], social affiliation orientations [chi2 (21, 193) = 29.44, p = .10], and social support [chi2 (68, 193) = 78.64, p = .18].
Variables and Measures

Four variables were used to address the research hypotheses: afterschool period MVPA was operationalized as caloric expenditure measured in Metabolic Equivalent (MET); and intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and social support were operationalized as level-2 predictors and measured at baseline and again at endpoint.
Intrinsic Motivation

Youths' PA intrinsic motivation at baseline and endpoint were measured using the Interest and Regulatory Motives Scale with higher mean scores across scale items indicating youth greater intrinsic enjoyment and degree of affective engagement in exercise. This questionnaire includes 9 items; each item is scored using a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (very false) to 5 (very true). An example item is "when I am active, it gives me energy." Previous studies have indicated adequate predictive validity and adequate concurrent validity of the Interest and Regulatory Motives Scale within similar demographic samples. This scale has demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency reliability (alpha = .93 to .94) based on the current data. The average scores were calculated to present youths' intrinsic motivation.
Social Affiliation Orientations

Youths' social affiliation orientation toward PA was assessed using the modified version of Social Motivational Orientations Scale for Sport (SMOSS) at baseline and endpoint. The original Social Motivational Orientations Scale for Sport (SMOSS) assesses youth's social affiliation orientation toward sports with higher mean scores indicating greater affiliation goals for PA participation. Previous empirical and psychometric studies have indicated adequate concurrent and predictive validity of the SMOSS within similar demographic samples. To fully capture youth's social affiliation orientation towards more general PA, the modified version replaced "sport" with "physical activity". An example item is "I make some good friends while participating in the physical activity." The average scores were calculated to present youths' social affiliation orientation. This questionnaire includes 7 items, each item is scored using a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree) and demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency reliability (alpha =. 89 to .91) based on the current data.
Social Support

Youths' reciprocal social support was assessed using a modified version of the Social Support and Exercise Survey at baseline and endpoint, with higher mean scores indicating greater reciprocal support with peers and program staff for PA. The original questionnaire examines support received by peers and program staff and includes 15 items, each item is scored using a 5-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (none) to 4 (very often). Previous empirical studies have indicated adequate concurrent and predictive validity of the Social Support and Exercise Survey within demographic samples. To fully capture reciprocal forms of social support, a targeted mechanism of the Connect positive social climate intervention, an additional four items were added that measured youth providing social support. These items mirrored the original scale items but were modified to ask about youth providing support rather than receiving it. An example item is "I reminded my family/friends and programs staff to be active (go outside and play)." In the current study, there was evidence of internal consistency of the modified Social Support and Exercise Survey, internal consistency reliability coefficient ranged from .87 to .94.
Physical Activity

Youths' afterschool period (3:00pm -6:00 pm) MVPA was measured using the Actigraph GT3X. For this study, accelerometers were worn on the non-dominant wrist for seven consecutive days during the afterschool period at baseline, midpoint, and endpoint. Ten second epoch lengths (count intervals) and cut points developed for youth were used to classify MVPA (> 3 metabolic equivalents). Accelerometer data was considered valid only if over 480 min (8h) of recorded data per day for at least 3 days were collected (based on criteria of previous study). Given the purpose of the current study, only afterschool hours (3pm-6pm) data were used to identify youth MVPA during the afterschool period.
Data Reduction

Accelerometry data were downloaded with ActiLife software and saved in a raw format containing acceleration data. These files were then read into R and summarized using the GGIR package using the Euclidean Norm Minus One metric and no imputation. Minutes of moderate PA was defined as an average acceleration between 201 and 707 mg and vigorous PA as an average acceleration > 707 mg, based on thresholds developed by.
Data Analysis

The data analyses followed four logical steps. First, the regression residual approach was used to assess youths' social-motivational mechanisms change scores. A descriptive analysis (mean and SD) was conducted to determine youths' afterschool period MVPA and average social-motivational mechanisms at each time point during the study. Then, the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was computed to determine if the equal variance assumption of the social-motivational variables was satisfied between schools. The ICCs results for the social-motivational variables were .08 for intrinsic motivation changes, .09 for social affiliation orientations changes, .06 for social support changes. These results indicated that between-school variability accounted for only between 6% to 9% of the variance in youths' scores for the social-motivational variables. Based on proposed threshold, an ICC < .10 suggests the equal variance assumption is not violated, using the individual scores for data analysis are appropriated. Thus, it was determined appropriate to construct with the individual score in level-2 model to determine the impact of social-motivational mechanisms on youth afterschool period MVPA when they were not grouped with their clusters. Thirdly, hierarchical linear modeling (HLM) analysis was conducted to address the two research hypotheses. Individual growth trajectories can be identified using HLM, which can handle unequal numbers of observation at each measurement. The HLM models that were tested are as follows:
Unconditional HLM model
An unconditional HLM model with no predictor was conducted to serve as a baseline model to determine the variance in afterschool MVPA between- and within- individual.
Hypothesis 1

A growth model (HLM 1) that included the time variable at level-1 of the equation was conducted to examine the average changing trajectory of youths' afterschool period MVPA across the 16-week intervention. The first time point was coded as 0, midpoint was coded as 1, and endpoint was coded as 2.
Hypothesis 2

A growth model (HLM 2) was conducted to examine the influences of PA intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientation, and social support on youths' changing MVPA trajectories. Thus, intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientation, and social support for PA were included in the level-2 model.

In hypothesis 2,  represents youths' afterschool period MVPA levels at the beginning of the intervention, while  represents the acceleration of the changing rate of youths' afterschool period MVPA over 16 weeks. The HLM analyses were conducted in the HLM software (Version 7.0, Skokie, IL). Lastly, restricted maximum likelihood estimation was used in the modeling to increase the precision of estimation due to the small sample size (Hox, 2010). Pseudo R2 was calculated using formula  to assess the amount of variance in afterschool period MVPA explained by predictors.
Results

Table 1 reports the mean, SDs, skewness, and Kurtosis indices for all variables. The results appear to indicate that on average participants' afterschool period MVPA, intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and social support tended to increase over the 16-week intervention. Table 2 presents correlations between the variables included in the model. ASP staffs' baseline MVPA was positively correlated to midpoint MVPA, endpoint MVPA, baseline intrinsic motivation, endpoint intrinsic motivation, and baseline social affiliation orientations. Baseline intrinsic motivation was positively correlated to endpoint intrinsic motivation. Baseline social affiliation orientations were positively correlated to endpoint social affiliation orientation. Baseline social support was positively correlated to endpoint social support.
HLM Results
The two proposed models were tested in sequence and results displayed in Table 3.
Unconditional HLM Model

The HLM 1 results showed that the overall average afterschool period MVPA across 16-weeks increased 29.55 minutes, which was significantly different from baseline MVPA. The between-individual variance  was 1.61, p > .05 and the within-individual variance  was 607.86, p > .05. ICC was calculated, rho = .0026, indicating .26% of the variance was accounted for by individual differences.
HLM Results for Hypothesis 1

With the time predictor added to the level-1 model, the time predictor slope was statistically significant (Coefficient = 18.97, t = 17.65, p < .001). Youth afterschool period MVPA increased, on average, 18.97 minutes in programme on the physical activity of 11 , p < .50, indicating the rates of change over the time in afterschool period MVPA did not differ across individuals. The effect size was large, pseudo R2 = .69, meaning 69% of the total variance in MVPA was explained by the time predictor.
HLM Results for Hypothesis 2

The HLM 2 results identified intrinsic motivation (coefficient = 3.02; p = .005), social affiliation orientations (coefficient = 2.83; p = .033) and social support (coefficient = 5.05; p < .001) as significant predictors of the afterschool MVPA changing trajectory. The effect size was large, pseudo R2 = .68, meaning 68% of the total variance in MVPA was explained by the time and social-motivational predictors.
Discussion

The social-motivational climate of a PA setting has been identified as a critical determinant of youth's PA participation. Still, there is a dearth of literature on the key mechanisms necessary for interventions to be effective for promoting positive youth PA behavior change over time in ASPs, especially among at-risk underserved young populations. Examination of the trajectory of youth MVPA change during the afterschool hours for youth participating in a social motivational intervention within their ASPs contributes to our understanding of the potential of social-motivational mechanisms for promoting PA engagement and recommended daily PA accrual among youth. The purpose of this study was to fill the knowledge gap by investigating the influences of intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and social support on underserved youths' afterschool period MVPA changing trajectories across a 16-week social-motivational PA intervention implemented within ASPs. The findings suggest that youth afterschool period MVPA increased, on average, 37.94 minutes in the 16-week intervention. Observed improvements in intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and social support resulting from the intervention positively and significantly predicted the youth afterschool period MVPA changing trajectory. Overall, these results help to clarify the role of the social-motivational climate in supporting youth social developmental needs and PA behavior change.

Previous intervention studies have predominantly focused on the changes in afterschool hours MVPA among general youth populations, and these findings were mixed. For example, found significant increases on third through fifth grade students' (8- 12 years old) MVPA from baseline to endpoint in a structured ASP that was focused on mastery support, while found no significant intervention effects on elementary school students MVPA using a similar intervention approach. The current study adds to this growing literature by focusing on underserved minority youth who are at greater risk of inactivity. The first research question investigated youth's average baseline and rate of afterschool period MVPA change trajectory across a 16-week social-motivational climate-based intervention within ASPs. In a cross-sectional study, found that on average, minority children (3rd to 5th graders; 8-12 years old) spent 21.7 minutes on MVPA during afterschool hours, which was significantly lower than the recommendation (30 minutes). Similarly, our baseline data showed that, on average, the underserved minority youth within our sample (9-15 years old) only spent 16.04 minutes on MVPA during afterschool hours compared to national averages.

These baseline data comparisons also demonstrate the significant evidenced-based declines in daily MVPA minutes with increasing age across childhood and adolescence. However, youth in the current study were successfully meeting and exceeding the benchmarks identified in policy guidelines for ASPs by the end of the social-motivational intervention. In particular, results of this study revealed a statistically significant increase, on average, from 16.04 minutes to 54.03 min of daily MVPA during the afterschool hours. Such changes are clinically significant for promoting the health of youth and are especially important for our sample of underserved youth who are less likely to have access to other supportive PA contexts (e.g., safe community park) and less likely to engage in 60 min of daily MVPA (Authors., 2015; 2020). Other previous PA interventions for youth that did not target social affiliation goals, intrinsic motivation, or reciprocal social support typically increased underserved youth MVPA, on average, between 4.93 minutes to 9.11 minutes. The current study found an increase of 37.94 minutes of daily PA among a sample of underserved youth, providing further evidence for the positive relations between a PA-supportive social-motivational climate and youth's PA behaviors in under-resourced ASPs.

However, a few previous ASP interventions that specifically aimed to increase youth MVPA through changes in the social-motivational climate documented some challenges with maintaining youth MVPA change throughout the intervention. The Trial of Activity for Adolescent Girls aimed to improve the daily MVPA of 8th grade girls through increased PA opportunities and social support the results showed that there were no differences in MVPA between the girls in the intervention or control group. The Active by Choice Trial (ACT) aimed to increase MVPA in underserved youth through building an ASP social climate that enhanced autonomy, fun, belongingness, and competence. The results showed that the students in the intervention condition engaged in 9.11 greater minutes of MVPA during the afterschool program period than control students at the midpoint, however, no significant effect of the intervention was found at 2-weeks post-intervention. Follow-up interviews with program staff of the ACT trial found several social barriers, including peer cliques, self-consciousness, and teasing impeded implementation and the long-term effectiveness of the intervention. The Connect through PLAY intervention, by design, addresses the social barriers found in previous social-motivational climate interventions, focused on increasing youth PA through supporting the social needs of adolescence including promoting friendship, social support, connection to peers and staff, belongingness, and social affiliation goals for PA. The findings of the current study not only expand on the previous ASP interventions that specifically aimed to increase youth MVPA by strengthening social-motivation climates, but also documented the sustaining MVPA changing trajectory in underserved youth during the 16-week intervention.

Given that intrinsic motivation, social affiliation orientations, and reciprocal social support positively predicted youth afterschool hour MVPA changing trajectory, facilitation of a social-motivational climate that targets these changes within youth PA settings is worth additional examination in future research. SDT argues that psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness should be supported for youth to be intrinsically motivated. In turn, intrinsic motivation has been shown to serve as both a promotive and protective factor, with previous research reporting youth daily PA accrual either continued increases or less decline over the adolescent and young adult years for those who maintained higher intrinsic motivation. To support and maintain intrinsic motivation in the PA sessions offered within ASPs, all Connect through PLAY activities, staff training and initiatives, and implementation strategies are intentionally designed to support autonomy, initiative and ownership over the PA programming, build connection and social support among youth and their peers and staff, and aid program staff in providing activities that adjusts to the skill levels of youth to promote competence. For example, The Connect Through PLAY intervention integrates free choice sessions and small-sided creative active play games and activities throughout each week of the programming where youth opt for and even work together to help design and deliver the Connect activities they would like to play. In the current study, youth intrinsic motivation slightly increased over the 16-week intervention and this change in intrinsic motivation led to sustained improvements in youth afterschool period MVPA. Results align with notion that the promotion of a supportive learning environment through a social-motivational climate that fosters intrinsic motivation can lead to sustained improvement in MVPA.

Likewise, increased social affiliation and social support mean scores from baseline to endpoint indicates that the Connect Through PLAY intervention's aim to facilitate close social relationships and having fun through PA with others was achieved and effective for changing youth social experiences and orientations towards PA. The social climate was built to improve PA affect, cognitions, and motivation for youth through meeting their developmental needs for social connection and support. The essential elements in the intervention (operationalized as moral, emotional and goal-oriented support; collaborative and cooperative PA activities centered on fun and friendship; equal treatment and access; and inclusive and engaging social norms and activities) focus on nurturing PA social affiliation at various levels (staff, youth, and activities) through building peer friendships, fostering group belonging, and enhancing staff connection through PA (Authors., 2020). The Connect intervention is believed to be one of the first studies to target social affiliation goals for PA and one of the few to implement a social-motivational climate intervention within pre-existing ASPs to foster intrinsic motivation and reciprocal social support, along with social affiliation goals, for promoting MVPA of underserved minoritized youth. The results of this study point to new promising mechanisms for developing effective PA interventions for early youth through optimizing social supports and social affiliation to meet social developmental and motivational needs.

While the present study provides insightful information about changing trajectories in at-risk youth afterschool period MVPA, it has limitations. First, participants in this study were youth between the ages of 9 to 15 years old and all from the southeastern United States, future studies should consider the generalizability to other regional and age samples. Second, it is also necessary to caution readers that the existing ASPs received continuous support by the research team to implement the intervention study throughout the 16-week period. Thus, to facilitate a similar positive social-motivational climate ASPs will need the support and training that was provided by the Connect Through PLAY research team. It is also important for future research to examine the key elements of a social-motivational climate approach that can facilitate the sustainability and generalizability of the findings. Lastly, future research with the full randomized controlled trial sample, which includes the active comparison, should be used to further determine the effects of the social-motivational climate on youth MVPA change upon the completion of the 5-year intervention.
Conclusions

Taken together, the results indicate that attention towards establishing a positive social-motivational climate that supports youth social developmental and motivational needs can have clinically significant impacts on youth MVPA accrual during the afterschool hours. ASPs provide supervision and care for 7.8 million children during the hours after school while parents are still at work and have been commissioned to support physical health and meet the PA benchmarks identified in policy guidelines as one part of a multi-component initiative to promote positive youth development. The Staff Comprehensive Training and the Staff Health Initiative components in the Connect through PLAY program provide necessary staff training and support that enhance staff motivation to establish a positive and inclusive environment for all enrolled youth. The findings advance our understanding of the role that the social-motivational climate can play in promoting youth MVPA within ASPs by clarifying the impact that a positive climate can have on youth afterschool period MVPA changing trajectory through increasing youth intrinsic motivation, social affiliation, and reciprocal social support. The findings of this study provide initial evidence that positive social-motivationally-based after school programming can lead to immediate PA behavior change during the afterschool period among underserved at-risk youth. To further operationalize a positive social motivational climate for promoting youth PA, additional studies that examine the mechanisms within this study (social affiliation goals, intrinsic motivation, reciprocal social support) and other potential mechanisms of a social-motivational climate that are effective for supporting youth PA behavior in ASPs change are needed.

passages.text: Evaluating a pilot, structured, face-to-face, antimicrobial stewardship, prospective audit-and-feedback program in emergency general surgery service in a community hospital
Background:

Prospective audit and feedback (PAF) is an established practice in critical care settings but not in surgical populations. We pilot-tested a structured face-to-face PAF program for our acute-care surgery (ACS) service.
Methods:

This was a mixed-methods study. For the quantitative analysis, the structured PAF period was from August 1, 2017, to April 30, 2019. The ad hoc PAF period was from May 1, 2019, to January 31, 2021. Interrupted time-series segmented negative binomial regression analysis was used to evaluate change in antimicrobial usage measured in days of therapy per 1,000 patient days for all systemic and targeted antimicrobials. Secondary outcomes included C. difficile infections, length of stay and readmission within 30 days. Each secondary outcome was analyzed using a logistic regression or negative binomial regression model. For the qualitative analyses, all ACS surgeons and trainees from November 23, 2015, to April 30, 2019, were invited to participate in an email-based anonymous survey developed using implementation science principles. Responses were measured using counts.
Results:

In total, 776 ACS patients were included in the structured PAF period and 783 patients were included in the in ad hoc PAF period. No significant changes in level or trend for antimicrobial usage were detected for all and targeted antimicrobials. Similarly, no significant differences were detected for secondary outcomes. The survey response rate was 25% (n = 10). Moreover, 50% agreed that PAF provided them with skills to use antimicrobials more judiciously, and 80% agreed that PAF improved the quality of antimicrobial treatment for their patients.
Conclusion:
Structured PAF showed clinical outcomes similar to ad hoc PAF. Structured PAF was well received and was perceived as beneficial by surgical staff.

Judicious antimicrobial use is necessary given the increasing rates of antimicrobial resistance worldwide combined with the lack of new antimicrobial agents in the drug-development pipeline.   The decision to use antimicrobials rests primarily on prescribers; therefore, education to bring prescribing behavior in line with current guidelines is essential for improving appropriate antimicrobial prescribing.   However, educational interventions have yielded mixed results. An Australian study showed no change in surgical prophylactic antibiotic prescribing,   and other studies showed reduction in antimicrobial use and improvements in antibiotic choice, timing, and duration.   Furthermore, surgeon compliance with antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP) recommendations is poor.   Therefore, there is an urgent need for formalized, structured approaches to optimizing antimicrobial therapy in the setting of surgical units.   It has been proposed that the best means to improve antimicrobial stewardship in general surgery should involve collaboration among different specialties, including prescribing surgeons.

Prospective audit and feedback (PAF) is an antimicrobial stewardship intervention that aims to maintain prescriber autonomy while increasing the capacity for prescribers to improve the use of antibiotics. Newly introduced PAF programs have been shown to reduce antimicrobial use and to improve patient outcomes.   PAF is more established in critical-care settings and is also used in medical and surgical populations. In one study, PAF in surgical populations led to early detection of inappropriate empirical antibiotic treatment as well as significant reductions in length of stay and duration of antimicrobial therapy.   Another study using PAF with surgeon participation showed a significant decrease in Pseudomonas aeruginosa prevalence, coupled with a significance increase in Klebsiella pneumoniae prevalence, as well as decreases in meropenem use and resistance.

At our institution, several ASP interventions have been implemented in the surgical population, including prescribing guidelines for common infections and ad hoc PAF for other surgical services. However, compliance with ASP recommendations by surgeons is poor.   Therefore, a more structured form of PAF was pilot tested at our institution, and outcomes were evaluated against ad hoc PAF.
Methods

The study was conducted at a 400-bed community teaching hospital in Toronto, Canada. An ASP was established at our institution in 2011 with a multimodal approach including PAF, development of guidelines and order sets, microbiology laboratory report optimization, and education. During the study period, staffing consisted of an ASP physician and 2 full-time-equivalent, ASP-trained pharmacists.

Structured PAF consisted of once-weekly, structured, face-to-face PAF with the acute-care surgery (ACS) service. This program was pilot tested from November 23, 2015, to April 30, 2019, at St. Joseph's Health Centre. The ACS service was chosen for this pilot program because the surgeons and residents do not start their surgeries until the afternoon and would be available for face-to-face PAF. The ACS service is responsible for patients with nonelective general surgery diagnoses (eg, appendicitis, cholecystitis, bowel obstruction, perforated viscus, etc) and was established in 2015 to streamline care for acutely ill patients in need of timely surgical intervention. These structured PAF sessions were attended primarily by the ASP pharmacist and ACS resident with occasional attendance from the ASP physician, the ACS staff physician, and/or the surgical ward pharmacist. These sessions lasted ~10-15 minutes on Monday mornings. The ASP pharmacist led these discussions by (1) identifying all ACS patients on antimicrobial therapy; (2) assessing indication for treatment and appropriateness of prescribed regimen based on relevant laboratory values, cultures, and imaging; and (3) making recommendations to optimize antimicrobial therapy. Starting April 30, 2019, structured PAF was stopped to assess effectiveness of this intervention. Structured PAF was initiated shortly after establishment of the ACS service; prestructured PAF data were lacking. Starting May 1, 2019, ad hoc PAF was reimplemented. It focused on select ACS patients on targeted antimicrobials highly associated with Clostridioides difficile infection and/or broad-spectrum antimicrobials: third-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenems, and clindamycin). This PAF occurred once to twice weekly. Recommendations were made to physicians using written methods (e-mail or note in patient's chart) or verbal methods (in-person or telephone).

In this mixed-methods study design, the qualitative study period was from November 2019 to February 2020 and quantitative study period was from August 1, 2017, to January 31, 2021. We sought to ascertain the surgeons' perceptions and experiences with structured PAF, to determine barriers and facilitators to structured PAF, and to evaluate the clinical outcomes of structured PAF compared to ad hoc PAF. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Board of Unity Health Toronto.
Quantitative study

A quasi-experimental design was used. All systemic antimicrobial orders prescribed by the ACS team from August 1, 2017, to January 31, 2021, were included. The structured PAF study period was from August 1, 2017, to April 30, 2019, whereas the ad hoc PAF period was from May 1, 2019, to January 31, 2021. The primary outcome was change in antimicrobial usage measured in days of therapy per 1,000 patient days (DOT/1,000 PD) for all antimicrobials and targeted antimicrobials ordered by the ACS service during the 21 months of structured PAF compared to the 21 months of ad hoc PAF. Targeted antimicrobials included third-generation cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, piperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenems, and clindamycin. Secondary outcomes were: (1) incidence of nosocomial Clostridioides difficile infection, (2) length of stay, and (3) readmission with 30 days during structured PAF period compared to ad hoc PAF period.

In terms of analysis, interrupted time-series, segmented, negative binomial regression   was used to evaluate the changes in antimicrobial usage for all antimicrobials and targeted antimicrobials during structured PAF period compared to ad hoc PAF period. The model parametrization   was used and included an offset equal to the natural log of the monthly number of patient days. For the secondary outcomes, a logistic regression model was used to evaluate nosocomial C. difficile infection and readmission within 30 days, and a negative binomial regression model used to evaluate length of stay.
Qualitative survey

All surgical residents, fellows, and staff surgeons who covered the ACS service from November 23, 2015, to April 30, 2019, were invited to participate by email with a link to an anonymous electronic survey (SurveyMonkey). The email provided information on the study, and completing the survey implied consent to participate in the study. The survey was developed by the investigator group and included 3 demographic questions, 3 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale, and 4 open-ended questions. The items explored surgeons' perceptions of structured face-to-face PAF and how their antimicrobial knowledge and quality of care for their patients have changed as a result. Quantitative data included data on length of surgical training and practice, number of antimicrobial stewardship rounds attended, attendees of rounds, and responses to the survey questions. Qualitative data included participants' free-text responses to the most and least useful aspect of structured PAF as well as barriers to and facilitators of judicious use of antimicrobials in surgery. We estimated the participant population to be 40, and we aimed for a response rate from at least 10 participants. A purposeful convenience sampling strategy was employed, and all survey respondents were included. In the analysis, counts and percentages were used for quantitative responses. Responses to free-text questions were analyzed and grouped into common categories.
Results
Quantitative study

We evaluated 776 ACS patients in the structured PAF period and 783 patients in the ad hoc PAF period. For the primary outcome (Table 1), there were no significant changes in level (RR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.70-1.02) or trend (RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.98-1.01) for all antimicrobials. Similarly, for targeted antimicrobials, there was no significant change in level (RR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.62-1.33) or trend (RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.96-1.02). The interrupted time-series, segmented, negative-binomial, regression analysis results are shown in Figures 1 and 2. In terms of secondary outcomes (Table 2), there were no significant differences in readmission with 30 days (OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.56-1.35), incidence of C. difficile infection (OR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.06-5.77) or length of stay (RR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.98-1.17).

Qualitative survey

The overall response rate was 25% (n = 10). With respect to demographics (Table 3), 60% of respondents were staff surgeons, and the rest were residents. Slightly more respondents had 7 or more years of practice (40%) compared to those with less years of practice (1-2 years and 3-4 years). All respondents attended 1-6 PAF session(s). Half of the respondents agreed that structured PAF provided them with skills to use antimicrobials more judiciously, and 80% of respondents agreed that structured PAF improved the quality of antimicrobial treatment for their patients (Fig. 3). Overall, 70% of respondents agreed that this pilot program should continue, and no respondent was against it. In terms of open-ended questions (Table 4), the most useful aspects of structured PAF served as a reminder to reassess duration and as a scheduled review of patients on antimicrobials. In contrast, respondents found the least useful aspects of face-to-face PAF to be the lack of a more formal structure and inconvenience of in-person rounds. In terms of barriers, respondents found it difficult to use antimicrobials judiciously due to lack of high-quality evidence, unique cases with lack of source control, and a high number of prescribers with differing prescribing habits. Conversely, improved dissemination of evidence-based guidelines based on local resistance rates was thought to facilitate judicious antimicrobial prescribing.

Discussion

To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare 2 models of PAF in the surgical population. The quantitative aspect of our study detected no significant changes in level or trend in antimicrobial usage for all antimicrobials and targeted antimicrobials when comparing face-to-face and ad hoc PAF. Additionally, there were no significant differences in any of the secondary outcomes. Previous studies comparing PAF to no PAF found reductions in antimicrobial usage and length of stay.   Taking this into account, our findings suggest that the format of PAF in surgical populations seems not to be as important as having some form of PAF. However, an important limitation of our study was the lack of a true preintervention period. Structured face-to-face PAF was pilot tested shortly after the establishment of the ACS service given the available ASP resources at the time. Therefore, no data representing antibiotic prescribing practices prior to PAF were available for comparison. Thus, sustained educational knowledge and judicious antimicrobial prescribing likely carried over to the ad hoc PAF period, which likely resulted in no difference in antimicrobial usage in both structured and ad hoc PAF periods. In addition, our study included only the surgical patients on the ACS team, who tend to have a short, uncomplicated admission compared to other surgical patients on non-ACS teams. Therefore, our study did not show a difference in length of stay with either format of PAF, compared to previous studies that included all surgical patients and compared PAF to no PAF.

Our qualitative survey found good support among respondents to continue structured face-to-face PAF because it facilitated knowledge and skills for judicious antimicrobial prescribing and optimized antimicrobial treatment for ACS patients. Given that 80% of respondents found that scheduled PAF improved antimicrobial usage but only 50% of respondents felt that they learned how to use antimicrobials more appropriately, there could be opportunities to further improve the educational goals of PAF among these prescribers. Additionally, it served as a reminder for the ACS team to reassess duration of antimicrobials for their patients. However, some respondents found the face-to-face structure inconvenient, and others preferred a more formal structure (ie, same time for PAF every Monday). Some barriers to judicious antimicrobial prescribing were similar to those reported in previous studies,   such as unique cases and difficulty in determining source control. Additionally, one barrier that was highlighted in our survey was the high number of prescribers (ie, turnover of surgical residents). These surgical residents may have varied prescribing practices and less exposure to PAF and its educational benefits given their relatively short time on the ACS service. Conversely, improved dissemination of evidence-based guidelines was thought to facilitate judicious antimicrobial prescribing. At our institution, guidelines on the management of surgical-site infections are readily available on our intranet homepage through a unique ASP icon. Another limitation of our study was the small number of survey respondents; therefore, perceptions of our face-to-face PAF pilot program could be further explored.

Structured face-to-face PAF showed similar clinical outcomes, including no change in antimicrobial usage, to ad hoc PAF for ACS patients at our institution. In addition, structured PAF appeared to be well received and perceived as beneficial by surgical staff. Other educational antimicrobial stewardship interventions in addition to ad hoc PAF can be explored to better support judicious antimicrobial use in emergency general surgery.

passages.text: Integrative analysis of the gut microbiota and faecal and serum short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites in patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy
Objective

The purpose of this study was to describe the changes in the gut microbiome of patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy (HE), as well as quantify the variations in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) and tryptophan metabolite levels in serum and faeces.
Methods

Fresh faeces and serum were collected from 20 healthy volunteers (NC group), 30 cirrhosis patients (Cir group), and 30 HE patients (HE group). Then, 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolite measurements were performed using the faeces. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry were used to measure SCFA and tryptophan levels, respectively. The results were analysed by SIMCA16.0.2 software. Differences in species were identified using MetaStat and t tests. The correlations among the levels of gut microbes and metabolites and clinical parameters were determined using Spearman correlation analysis.
Results

Patients with cirrhosis and HE had lower microbial species richness and diversity in faeces than healthy volunteers; these patients also had altered beta-diversity. Serum valeric acid levels were significantly higher in the HE group than in the Cir group. Serum SCFA levels did not differ between the Cir and NC groups. Serum melatonin and 5-HTOL levels were significantly higher in the HE group than in the Cir group. The Cir and NC groups had significant differences in the levels of eight serum tryptophan metabolites. Furthermore, the levels of faecal SCFAs did not differ between the HE and Cir groups. Faecal IAA-Ala levels were significantly lower in the HE group than in the Cir group. There were significant differences in the levels of 6 faecal SCFAs and 7 faecal tryptophan metabolites between the Cir and NC groups. Certain gut microbes were associated with serum and faecal metabolites, and some metabolites were associated with certain clinical parameters.
Conclusion

Reduced microbial species richness and diversity were observed in patients with HE and cirrhosis. In both serum and faeces, the levels of different SCFAs and tryptophan metabolites showed varying patterns of change. In HE patients, the levels of some serum tryptophan metabolites, and not SCFAs, were correlated with liver function and systemic inflammation. Systemic inflammation in patients with cirrhosis was correlated with faecal acetic acid levels. In summary, this study identified metabolites important for HE and cirrhosis.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12967-023-04262-9.
Introduction

Liver cirrhosis is a serious type of chronic liver disease that often results in high rates of morbidity and mortality. Liver-related complications, such as hepatic encephalopathy (HE), which can affect multiple organs outside the liver, are the primary cause of death among individuals with this condition. HE is a neuropsychiatric disorder that is associated with acute or chronic liver disease and is characterized by varying degrees of cognitive and fine motor impairments, such as inattentiveness, blunted affect, impaired memory, reversed sleep-wake cycle, tremors, myoclonus, asterixis, and deep tendon hyperreflexia. Epidemiological studies have revealed that the prevalence of HE is increasing globally. As a result, it is crucial to prevent or treat HE as early as possible to enhance prognosis. However, the pathogenesis of HE is a complex and poorly understood process that includes hyperammonaemia, inflammation, changes to the gut microbiota, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neurotransmitter abnormalities. Unfortunately, no single factor has been shown to fully explain the pathogenesis of HE, which leads to poor treatment outcomes and prognosis.

Ammonia and inflammation are key factors involved in the pathophysiologic development of HE. Recent studies have shown that patients with cirrhosis have an imbalanced intestinal flora. These changes can lead to the excessive production of ammonia, resulting in hyperammonaemia. Additionally, alterations in the gut microbiota have been shown to promote the production of endotoxins, leading to both systemic and neurological inflammation. These findings suggest a strong correlation between alterations in the gut microbiota and the onset of HE in individuals with cirrhosis. Several previous studies have also reported a notable alteration in the microbiota structure among patients with HE. However, importantly, the function and effects of bacteria can vary greatly based on the phyla or family.

In patients with cirrhosis and HE, the gut microbiota undergoes alterations, and there is also a change in the shared metabolic processes that occur between the host and microbiota. Research has shown that patients with HE exhibit a decline in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels in their intestinal tract due to a reduction in the levels of SCFA-producing species (such as Anaerostipes caccae). Low levels of SCFAs can contribute to the development of HE by enhancing the transfer of neurotoxins, weakening intestinal barrier function, and increasing intestinal barrier permeability. Furthermore, a correlation has been observed between reduced serum SCFA levels and cirrhosis; however, different SCFAs serve various functions; for example, butyrate primarily targets colonocytes to generate energy, while propionate is mainly transported to the liver, where it promotes gluconeogenesis. Only butyrate exhibits significant epigenetic properties that are involved in various diseases. Understanding the clinical importance of SCFAs by assessing alterations in their levels may provide a new perspective for understanding the pathogenesis of HE and may provide more options for its treatment. Nevertheless, few studies have explored the relationship between both faecal and serum SCFAs and cirrhosis or HE to date.

Additionally, certain metabolites of tryptophan, namely, indoleacetic acid (IAA) and indolepropionic acid (IPA), have been shown to impact intestinal permeability and immune function. A recent study suggested that alterations in tryptophans may contribute to the development of inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, and neuropsychiatric disorders. The liver plays a crucial role in the metabolism of tryptophan, and any disruptions in this process can result in fluctuations in the levels of its metabolites. These fluctuations can potentially impact the functioning of the central nervous system. As HE has neurological and psychiatric symptoms, tryptophan metabolites may also be closely related to HE. Nevertheless, there is currently no research exploring the connection between tryptophan metabolites and cirrhosis or HE.

In the context of the information presented above, our study aimed to provide a comprehensive description of the alterations in the gut microbiome of individuals with cirrhosis or HE and to quantitatively evaluate the alterations in the levels of SCFAs and tryptophans in both serum and faeces. Additionally, we explored the correlation between the gut microbiota and these two types of metabolites, the relationship between the levels of these two types of metabolites in the serum and faeces of cirrhosis and HE patients, and their correlation with clinical parameters.
Materials and methods
Research subjects, selection criteria, and exclusion criteria

Healthy volunteers (NC group), overt HE (OHE) patients (HE group), and patients with cirrhosis but without HE (Cir group) were recruited at the Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University (Guizhou Province, China) from January to December 2022. Written consent was provided by all participants before the collection of specimens. Faeces and blood samples were collected from all participants to characterize the gut microbiota, faecal metabolites (SCFAs and tryptophans), and serum metabolites (SCFAs and tryptophans). Healthy volunteers were selected based on the following assessments: medical history, physical examination, chest X-ray, routine blood tests, blood glucose, liver function, kidney function, and other physical and chemical examinations, which revealed no diseases of the brain, heart, lung, liver, kidney, or other major organ systems. A liver biopsy, the discovery of varices or portal hypertension, or the decompensation of chronic liver disease were all used to diagnose liver cirrhosis. HE was diagnosed according to the 2014 AASLD/EASL HE guidelines. OHE was determined to be Grade II or higher HE based on features such as disorientation, somnolence, and coma-like symptoms. Patients with diabetes, mental illness, hepatocellular carcinoma, primary sclerosing cholangitis, autoimmune hepatitis, gastrointestinal diseases, and a history of gastrointestinal surgery were excluded. Additionally, patients who underwent hormone replacement therapy or used antipsychotic medication, antibiotics, or probiotics within the 6 weeks prior to the study, as well as patients with active alcohol use disorder (AUDIT-10 > 8), were excluded. This study was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of Helsinki's Declaration and received approval from the Medical Ethics Committee of Guizhou Medical University (Ethics No. 2020007).

passages.text: Sample collection and processing

Fresh faeces (200-300 mg) from patients and volunteers were collected into two separate disposable sterile 5 mL tubes. One tube was used to sequence the gut microbiota, and the other was used to detect metabolites. Each sterile tube was labelled, placed in an ice box, and then transferred to the laboratory. Subsequently, specimens used for the detection of metabolites were frozen in liquid nitrogen for one minute before being kept at - 80  C. The next morning, peripheral venous fasting blood from each participant was drawn and collected in tubes that were then labelled. Blood was then centrifuged to obtain the serum, and 0.5 mL of serum was placed in 1.5 mL centrifuge tubes. Before usage, the sera sample tubes were labelled and kept at - 80  C. Clinical information was obtained from patients, and basic information was obtained from volunteers.
Targeted metabolomics study
Short-chain fatty acids
Extraction of serum metabolites

A 100 microL serum sample along with two internal standards (0.2 mL of 2-methylpentanoic acid and 0.05 mL of 50% H2SO4) were put into an Eppendorf (EP) tube. The mixture was shaken for 10 min, spun for 30 s, and then sonicated in an ice bath for 10 min. Following a 15-min centrifugation at 10,000 rpm, the mixture was kept at - 20  C for 30 min. The supernatant was collected for gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS).
Extraction of faecal metabolites

A 100 mg faecal sample diluted in 1 ml of distilled water was placed in an EP tube, vortexed, shaken, homogenized, and sonicated. Subsequently, the material was centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 20 min. Then, 0.8 mL of the supernatant, 0.1 mL of H2SO4 (50%), and 0.8 mL of 2-methylpentanoic acid were added to the tube, followed by vortexing and sonication. The sample was kept at - 20  C for 30 min after being centrifuged for 15 min at 10,000 rpm. The supernatant was finally collected for GC-MS analysis.
GC-MS analysis

The GC-mass spectrometer used for the GC-MS analysis was a SHIMADZU GC2030-QP2020 NX. GC-MS analysis followed the protocols of previous work. All equipment information and the detailed methodology for GC-MS are available in the Additional file 3: Methods.
Tryptophan
Extraction of serum metabolites

A 100 microL serum sample and 400 microL of extract solution were placed in an EP tube, vortexed, shaken, and sonicated before being kept at - 40  C for an hour. A new EP tube was used to collect 400 microL of the supernatant after centrifugation (12,000 rpm; 15 min). This supernatant was then dried in nitrogen and redissolved in 100 microL of an aqueous solution containing 0.1% formic acid. To recover the supernatant for ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) analysis, the supernatant was centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min.
Extraction of faecal metabolites

A 50 mg faecal sample was mixed with 500 microL extract solution in an EP tube. The mixture was vortexed, shaken, homogenized, sonicated, and allowed to sit at -40  C for 1 h. Then, 320 microL of supernatant was transferred to a fresh EP tube, dried in nitrogen, and redissolved in an 80 microL volume of aqueous solution. The supernatant was centrifuged and collected for UHPLC-MS/MS analysis.
UHPLC-multiple reaction monitoring (MRM)-MS analysis

The target compounds were separated on a Waters ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 liquid chromatography column using an EXIONLC System (SCIEX) (Sciex, Framingham, MA, USA). UHPLC-MRM-MS analysis was performed according to previous studies. All equipment information and software and the detailed methodology for UHPLC-MRM-MS are available in the Additional file 3: Methods
DNA extraction, 16S rRNA amplification, and sequencing

Using the CTAB/SDS technique, total genomic DNA was isolated from the samples. Using 515 F-806R primers, the 16 S rRNA genes in various locations were amplified. The amplification of 16S rRNA and the quality assessment of polymerase chain reaction products were performed following the protocol of a previous study. Illumina sequencing libraries were created using the NEBNext  UltraTM IIDNA Library Prep Kit (Cat No. E7645). The quality of the libraries was assessed using a Qubit@ 2.0 fluorometer from Life Technologies GmbH in Darmstadt, Germany, and an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system from Agilent Technologies in Waldbronn, Germany. The libraries were sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq platform in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions (Illumina Inc., San Diego, USA).
Follow-up study

Telephone conversations with patients or members of their immediate families were conducted for follow-up. The follow-up period was 90 days after discharge. The endpoints of this study comprised mortality associated with cirrhosis or HE, recurrence, and readmission related to cirrhosis or HE.
Statistical analysis
Clinical parameters

SPSS 26.0 software was used to conduct a statistical analysis of clinical parameters. A normality test was first performed on continuous variables. Quantitative normal variables are presented as the mean +- SD. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare variables with uneven variance, whereas the t test was used to compare data with normal variance homogeneity. When comparing groups, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was utilized, and the median was used to present nonnormal variables. A chi-square test was used to compare groups, and the grade values are reported as a frequency in percentages. A statistically significant difference was considered when the P value was lower than 0.05.
Sequencing data analysis

Initial amplicon sequence variations (ASVs) were denoised using QIIME2 software (version QIIME2-202006), and ASVs with an abundance of less than 5 were filtered out. Taxonomic assignment was also performed using QIIME2. Using a sequence-number standard based on the sample with the fewest sequences, the absolute abundance of the ASVs was normalized. The generated normalized data were used to calculate the diversity indices. Chao1, Shannon, and Simpson were used to evaluate the diversity, while Pielou's evenness index was employed to evaluate the diversity, richness, and consistency of the microbial community. Based on weighted and unweighted UniFrac distances, the beta diversity was estimated.

Using principal component analysis (PCA), a cluster analysis was performed. To visualize the differences in the complicated multidimensional data between samples, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was performed. To overcome the constraints of linear models (PCA and PCoA), nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) based on the Bray-Curtis distance was carried out. To examine variations in community structure between groups, the adonis and anosim functions in QIIME2 were employed. Identification of species with significant differences in each classification level was performed using MetaStat and t tests in R software v3.5.3. Identification of biomarkers was performed using LEfSe analysis (LDA score = 4) with LEfSe software v1.0. Additionally, functional annotation analysis using PICRUSt2 software version 2.1.2-b was carried out to determine the variations in community function between various groups.
Targeted metabolomics data analysis

Multivariate data containing the sample name, the compound name, and concentration details were analysed using SIMCA v16.0.2 software (Umetrics, Malmo, Sweden). To reduce noise and significant variations in the variables, the data were scaled and logarithmically transformed. After these adjustments, PCA was used to show the distribution and categorization of the samples. Outliers in the dataset were determined by using the 95% confidence interval in the PCA score plot. By using an orthogonal partial least squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA), the model's dependability was assessed, and its evaluation indices (R2 and Q2) were determined by running seven cross-validations. The list of 31 tryptophan metabolites and their abbreviations are summarized in Additional file 1: Table S5.
Spearman correlation analysis

The correlation between the levels of gut microbes, SCFAs, and tryptophans and between these two types of metabolites and clinical parameters was determined using SPSS 26.0. The correlations between these features was visualized using the pheatmap package in R software.
Results
Characterization of participants

Initially, 106 specimens were collected from 86 patients and 20 healthy volunteers. According to our exclusion criteria, 21 patients were excluded, and five patients were not assessed. Finally, the entire sample size was 80 subjects, including 30 HE patients (HE group), 30 cirrhosis patients (Cir group), and 20 healthy volunteers (NC group). The HE, Cir, and NC groups differed significantly in age (p < 0.001). The ages in both the HE group (56.13 +- 13.20) and the Cir group (52.23 +- 9.00) were higher than that in the NC group (44.45 +- 8.46). The difference between the HE and Cir groups, however, was not statistically significant (p = 0.161). Notably, the three groups did not differ significantly in sex, body mass index (BMI), or aetiology (p = 0.888, 0.900, and 0.566, respectively). Patient Child-Pugh scores were lower in the Cir group than in the HE group (p = 0.005). A higher model for end-stage liver disease score (Meld-score) was observed in the HE group (19.67 +- 5.96) than in the Cir group (13.90 +- 6.51). The HE group (70%) had a greater prevalence of moderate to severe ascites than the Cir group (26.67%). The rate of previous variceal haemorrhage was higher in the HE group (43.33%) than in the Cir group (16.67%). The HE group (43.33%) had a higher prevalence of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunts (TIPS) than the Cir group (6.67%). A total of 36.67% of the participants in the HE group had spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, compared to 10.00% in the Cir group. The HE group had higher total bilirubin (TBIL), direct bilirubin (DBIL), indirect bilirubin (IBIL), prothrombin time (PT), international normalized ratio (INR), and ammonia levels than the Cir group, whereas alanine transaminase (ALT) and aspartate transaminase (AST) levels were lower in the HE group. There were no statistically significant differences between the proportions of 90-day mortality and 90-day recurrence in the HE group and the Cir group (13.33% and 16.67%, vs. 0% and 0%, respectively) (Table 1).
